title: Hierarchical Communication
summary: Analyze hierarchical AllReduce by separating input shard size, sent volume, aggregate node traffic, and available port capacity.

blocks.md:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Analyze hierarchical AllReduce by separating input shard size, sent volume, aggregate node traffic, and available port capacity
- Analyze how dimension-ordered reduction on torus topologies reduces latency hop complexity from multiplicative volume to additive perimeter
- Explain the mechanics of rail-optimized routing and diagnose the performance penalties caused by topology-unaware rank placement
- Identify how in-network reduction (SHARP) offloads collective arithmetic to switch ASICs to eliminate store-and-forward GPU memory traffic
- Order the three causal phases of Hierarchical AllReduce across intra-node and inter-node network tiers

blocks.source: Vol II, Collective Communication, § Hierarchical Communication
blocks.md: The AllReduce cost models in a later section assume a flat network with uniform endpoint bandwidth, whereas real clusters expose the tiered bandwidth hierarchy of a later section. Because intra-node links are abundant and fast while inter-node links are scarce and expensive, hierarchical communication shrinks payloads locally before they cross the scarce tier, decomposing AllReduce into a local ReduceScatter, a cross-node reduction, and a local AllGather.

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md:
In the book this section runs through:

- Hierarchical AllReduce
- Multidimensional reduction on a torus
- In-network reduction with SHARP
- Topology-aware routing

Pay attention to: The bandwidth hierarchy: intra-node NVLink (450 GB/s one-way) vs inter-node InfiniBand NDR (50 GB/s per port); Three-phase Hierarchical AllReduce: intra-node ReduceScatter, inter-node AllReduce on M/G shards, intra-node AllGather; In-network reduction (SHARP): aggregation in switch ASICs eliminating GPU store-and-forward latency and memory traffic; Topology-aware routing: Dimension-ordered reduction on 3D torus TPU pods.

blocks.prompt: Think first: Describe the architectural principle of rail-optimized routing in multi-GPU DGX clusters, and explain the performance pathology that occurs if a job scheduler assigns process ranks without topology awareness.
blocks.md: Rail-aware placement keeps the same model shard at the same local GPU index across replicas, aligning corresponding-rank communication with GPU-to-NIC affinities. Distinct shard groups can then use distinct rails when the topology provides them. A poor mapping may concentrate traffic on a subset of NICs or cross additional fabric tiers. Alignment does not reserve bandwidth, eliminate contention, or imply a universal slowdown factor; measure the actual placement.

questions.q: On an 8-node cluster with 8 GPUs per node, fast local NVLink, and eight independent 50 GB/s network ports per node, how can hierarchical AllReduce improve on a flat ring whose inter-node traffic is serialized through one port?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. Each inter-node rank receives an input shard of $M/8$, then sends \$2(7/8)(M/8)$ bytes in its eight-node ring and receives the same volume. Summing over eight local ranks gives \$2(7/8)M$ sent per node, not an eightfold reduction in aggregate optical bytes. Speedup comes from the declared local aggregation and independent-port mapping; a topology-aware flat implementation can change the comparison.
questions.hint: Think about: analyze hierarchical AllReduce by separating input shard size, sent volume, aggregate node traffic, and available port capacity.
options: Hierarchical AllReduce converts the floating-point values to 8-bit integers during the intra-node phase to save inter-node bandwidth.
Flat Ring AllReduce requires every GPU to establish an optical fiber connection directly to all 63 other GPUs in the cluster.
Local ReduceScatter creates one 125 MB shard per GPU from a 1 GB tensor; corresponding-rank AllReduces can distribute these shards across the eight ports, followed by local AllGather.
Hierarchical AllReduce executes without any inter-node network synchronization barriers.

questions.q: How does dimension-ordered reduction on a 3D torus network (such as Google TPU pods) optimize communication latency and link utilization compared to running a single global logical ring?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. Sequential full-message rings along X, Y, and Z reduce startup rounds from \$2(XYZ-1) to \$2[(X-1)+(Y-1)+(Z-1)]. Their bandwidth time is \$2M[(X-1)/X+(Y-1)/Y+(Z-1)/Z]/beta, not the cost of one global ring. Direct-neighbor routing avoids arbitrary paths but does not eliminate other workloads' contention. Skipping an axis omits contributions; a central root recreates a bottleneck.
questions.hint: Think about: analyze how dimension-ordered reduction on torus topologies reduces latency hop complexity from multiplicative volume to additive perimeter.
options: It skips communication along the Z-axis by projecting all activations onto a 2D plane.
It executes axis-aligned rings in sequence, reducing startup rounds to \$2[(X-1)+(Y-1)+(Z-1)] while trading extra full-message transfers for shorter rings.
It broadcasts full gradient tensors directly to all pod nodes simultaneously over optical circuit switches.
It routes all collective packets through a single central root TPU in the pod to minimize total wire length.

questions.q: On a supported aggregation path, SHARP can move intermediate reduction arithmetic from endpoints into switches, but the resulting latency and training-step benefit still depend on message size, placement, switch resources, and exposed dependencies.
questions.explanation: True. Aggregation-capable switches combine contributions in the packet path, avoiding some intermediate endpoint receive-reduce-forward work. Startup, switch processing, data movement, and contention remain. The supported operation and datatype, aggregation-resource availability, and binding links determine collective benefit; independent computation and consumer readiness determine how much reaches step time. In-network reduction does not guarantee a fixed speedup for every tensor.

questions.q: Sequence the three phases of Hierarchical AllReduce executed across a multi-node cluster with $G$ GPUs per node:
questions.explanation: The correct order is: (3) intra-node ReduceScatter across local GPUs over NVLink leaving each GPU holding \$1/G of the partially reduced tensor, (2) inter-node AllReduce across corresponding GPU positions over InfiniBand on the M/G node shards, (1) intra-node AllGather across local GPUs over NVLink to reconstruct the full globally reduced tensor. The hierarchy first exploits high-speed intra-node NVLink to reduce local data into shards; then performs the expensive inter-node exchange only on the reduced M/G payload over InfiniBand; and finally redistributes the global results locally over NVLink.
questions.hint: Think about: order the three causal phases of Hierarchical AllReduce across intra-node and inter-node network tiers.
items: intra-node ReduceScatter across local GPUs over NVLink leaving each GPU holding \$1/G of the partially reduced tensor.
inter-node AllReduce across corresponding GPU positions over InfiniBand on the $M/G$ node shards
intra-node AllGather across local GPUs over NVLink to reconstruct the full globally reduced tensor
